title: 【社説】国会前や街角で、憲法を呼ぶ声がする　デモを政治の参照点に
extracted_text: ●「戦争」の予感が、人々を9条改憲反対デモへと駆り立てている●人類には、戦争放棄や武力行使禁止を目指してきた歴史がある。憲法を今こそ掲げたい●政府は、声を上げる人々の懸念と期待に向き合って欲しい 憲法を呼ぶ声が聞こえる。国会前や全国の街角で、政府に憲法を守れと求め、9条の改憲に反対するデモが相次いでいる。 為政者を縛り、個人個人の侵されてはならない権利を定めた憲法は、日本の民主主義の「骨格」だ。普段はそう意識することのない憲法を、思い出さざるを得ないのは、そこに書かれた原則や権利が脅かされている時だ。 デモに中学の同級生と参加した20代女性は「学校で教わって以来、憲法を誇りに思ってきた」と話した。1人で来た30代女性は「そのまま変わらずにあるものかと」。 プラカードを持ち静かに座っている人がいる。リズムにのって思い切り声を出す人がいる。しゃぼん玉を飛ばす人がいる。それぞれが守りたい日常を象徴する光景がある。 衆議院で単独3分の2を占める自民党が掲げる改憲4項目には9条が含まれ、与党内の日本維新の会など、他にも改憲に肯定的な勢力がある。 近年進められてきた、防衛費増額、南西諸島での自衛隊の増強、武器輸出政策の転換。そこに始まった米・イスラエルのイラン攻撃と、米トランプ大統領による自衛隊派遣要請。そうした状況が、人々に「身近に戦争が迫っている」と予感させる。平和国家として戦争を止めるどころか、「加害する側になるかもしれない」と懸念させる。「防波堤である9条を変えさせるわけにはいかない」という、国民主権を担う市民としての責任感が、人々をデモへと駆り立てる。 日本国憲法は、戦争のない世界を目指す普遍的な理想や国内外の努力の歴史の上にあるものだ。第1次世界大戦後に戦争放棄を明記した不戦条約や、第2次大戦後に武力による威嚇や武力行使を原則禁止した国連憲章の精神が、前文や9条には脈打っている。 戦争のない世界は今も実現していない。平和主義は規範として掲げれば実現するわけではない。9条が、戦争をしない状態を自動的に作り出すわけではない。 ただ、現在の情勢の中で、日本が平和主義を掲げ続けることが、国際社会に訴えるものは大きいはずだ。私たちは、人類が挑んできた困難な挑戦の最前線にいる。 デモは、憲法上の当然の権利であるだけでなく、世界的にもごく一般的な意見表明の手段だ。政治家は、デモという手法を馬鹿にしたり警戒したりしている場合ではない。声を上げる人々の懸念に向き合い、期待に応えることができているか。それを参照点に政治と外交を進めて欲しい。
translated_text: A premonition of "war" is driving people to demonstrate against constitutional revision of Article 9. Humanity has a history of pursuing the abolition of war and the prohibition of the use of armed force. Now is the time to uphold the constitution. The government should address the concerns and expectations of people raising their voices. Voices calling for the constitution are heard. In front of the Diet and on street corners across the country, demonstrations are occurring one after another, demanding that the government protect the constitution and opposing revision of Article 9. The constitution, which binds those in power and establishes the inviolable rights of individuals, is the "skeleton" of Japanese democracy. Normally we are not aware of it, but we are reminded of the constitution when the principles and rights written in it are threatened. A woman in her twenties who participated in the demonstration with her middle school classmates said, "I've been proud of the constitution since learning about it in school." A woman in her thirties who came alone said, "I wonder if it will stay the same as it is now." Some sit quietly holding placards. Some shout at the top of their lungs to a rhythm. Some blow soap bubbles. There are scenes symbolizing the daily lives each person wants to protect. The Liberal Democratic Party, which alone holds a two-thirds majority in the House of Representatives, has included Article 9 among its four items for constitutional revision, and there are other forces favoring revision, such as the Japan Innovation Party within the ruling coalition. In recent years, there have been increases in defense spending, reinforcement of the Self-Defense Forces in the southwestern islands, and a shift in weapons export policies. Then came the US-Israel attacks on Iran, and US President Trump's request for the dispatch of the Self-Defense Forces. Such developments give people a premonition that "war is approaching nearby." Instead of stopping war as a peaceful nation, there is concern that Japan "may become the perpetrators." A sense of responsibility as citizens who bear popular sovereignty, feeling that "Article 9 as a breakwater cannot be changed," drives people to demonstrate. The Constitution of Japan is built on the universal ideals of pursuing a world without war and the history of efforts both domestically and abroad. The spirit of the Treaty of Paris, which after World War I expressly renounced war, and the United Nations Charter, which after World War II prohibited threats or use of force in principle, pulses in the preamble and Article 9. A world without war has not yet been achieved. Merely upholding pacifism as a norm will not make it a reality. Article 9 does not automatically create a state of non-war. However, in the current situation, Japan continuing to uphold pacifism should have a significant message for the international community. We are at the forefront of the difficult challenges humanity has faced. Demonstrations are not only a natural right under the constitution but also a very common means of expressing opinion worldwide. Politicians should not belittle or be wary of the method of demonstration. They should use as a reference point whether they can address the concerns of people raising their voices and meet their expectations as they advance politics and diplomacy.
title_en: Voices Calling for the Constitution Heard in Front of the Diet and on Street Corners - Demonstrations as a Political Reference Point
